sents.text: As your data grows, your workbench grows with it, in five steps.
Step one: Google Colab with Google Drive, free in your browser.
Step two: Python on your own laptop.
Step three: a dev container, which is the exact same setup packed into a box, so it runs identically anywhere.
Step four: Databricks Free Edition, for real big data with Spark.
And step five: the BigQuery sandbox, for running SQL on huge public datasets.
You don't need all five today.
Each one arrives in the course that needs it.
Why five steps?
Because the right tool depends on the size of your data.
Small data fits in your computer's memory, and Colab or a laptop handles it easily.
Medium data, tens of gigabytes, still works on a laptop with fast tools like DuckDB and Polars.
Big data needs many machines working together, and that's what Spark clusters do.
And very big data, terabytes, lives in cloud warehouses.
Same habits, bigger tools.
And every step matches something used in real companies.
Colab is a cousin of the hosted notebooks big cloud providers sell.
Your laptop setup is a developer's workstation.
Dev containers are how teams make sure everyone runs the same environment.
Databricks is used by thousands of companies for data engineering.
And BigQuery is a cloud data warehouse.
So when you finish this series, you won't just know AI.
You'll already know the tools of the job.
Here's a promise.
The offline tools, Python, VS Code, Jupyter and Git, are open source.
They're free, and they're yours forever, whatever any company decides.
The online tools are free tiers, and their limits can change.
That's exactly why your work lives in GitHub.
If one service changes its rules, you simply carry on somewhere else.
